summary: The hypothesis that multi-restart simulated annealing (best-of-3 runs with shuffled greedy initialization) would outperform a single long SA run was refuted. Mean scores were 84.53 (multi-restart) vs 84.34 (single-run), a difference of +0.19 points — well within the ±2-point judge variance and not statistically meaningful.
key_points: h-main (multi-restart SA, 3×2.5s runs): scores 84.14, 86.01, 83.43 (mean 84.53). h-ablation (single SA, 1×7s run): scores 83.73, 82.94, 86.36 (mean 84.34). The 0.19-point gap is noise — h-ablation's best single run (86.36) beat all h-main runs.

Key insight: SA convergence time matters more than starting-point diversity. The SA neighborhood moves (expand-to-limit, target-aware adjustments) are effective enough to escape the initial greedy layout, so shuffled greedy orderings provide no measurable advantage.

Both approaches plateau around 83–86 on the judge. To break past this ceiling, future iterations should investigate fundamentally different strategies — e.g., better neighborhood operators, constraint-aware placement heuristics, or hybrid approaches — rather than tuning restart mechanics.
Current best score observed across all runs: 86.36 (from the single-run SA ablation arm).
